questions_and_answers.question_text: What does a reflexive pronoun indicate in a sentence?

answers.answer: The subject is doing the action to others
The subject and object are the same person

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which German reflexive pronoun is used for third‑person subjects?
In the sentence 'Meine Frau kann sich nicht an das Klima gewöhnen', what is the function of 'sich'?

answers.answer: It is the indirect object referring to another person
It is the object referring to the same person as the subject

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which pronoun does German use when the subject is 'ich' and a reflexive pronoun is needed?
In which case can 'sich' serve when the subject is third person?
What pronoun do you use after the preposition 'von' if the subject is 'ich'?
Which set of subjects would trigger the reflexive pronoun 'sich'?
What is the reflexive pronoun in the sentence 'Wir möchten uns gern einige Bücher leihen'?
What does the phrase 'Er spricht immer nur von sich' mean?

answers.answer: He always talks only about himself

questions_and_answers.question_text: When the subject of a sentence is 'wir', which pronoun is used for reflexive constructions after prepositions?

articles.text:
In many sentences the object of the verb, the thing or person acted upon, is the same as the subject or doer.  We say, for example, in English: Mr. Wilson introduced himself.  Or: She thinks a good deal of herself, doesn't she?  The identity of subject and object in English is indicated by adding the suffix –self to the pronoun designating the object.  Pronouns of this kind are called Reflexive Pronouns.

The German Reflexive Pronoun

In German, as in English, the subject and object of a verb may be the same.  Note the following examples from your basic sentences:

Meine Frau kann sich nicht an das Klima gewöhnen.
Darf ich mir mal Ihre Zeitung leihen?
Möchten Sie sich mal eins meiner Bücher leihen?

My wife can't get (herself) used to the climate.
May I borrow (lend myself) your newspaper?
Would you like to borrow one of my books?

In sentence (a) the object of the verb refers to the same person as the subject and has the form sich.  In sentence (b) the interested bystander or indirect object of the verb is the same person as the subject and has the form mir.  In sentence (c) the indirect object of the verb is the same person as the subject and has the form sich.

German has only one reflexive pronoun, the form sich, meaning 'himself, herself, itself, yourself, yourselves, themselves'.  It occurs wherever the subject of the verb is er, sie, Sie or es, or is a noun which can be replaced by these pronouns.

Herr Allen kann sich nicht an das Klima gewöhnen.
Herr Allen und seine Frau können sich nicht an das Klima gewöhnen.
Können Sie sich nicht an das Klima gewöhnen?

Mr. Allen can't get (himself) used to the climate.
Mr. Allen and his wife can't get (themselves) used to the climate.
Can't you get (yourself) used to the climate?

The reflexive pronoun sich may function either as the object or as the interested bystander in a sentence.  We might say it can have either an Accusative or Dative function.  Compare the sentences above with the following:

Möchten Sie sich ein Buch leihen?
Er möchte sich ein Buch leihen.

Wherever the subject of the sentence can be replaced by ich or wir German uses the regular pronoun forms mich, mir and uns.

Ich kann mich nicht an das Klima gewöhnen.
Meine Frau und ich können uns nicht an das Klima gewöhnen.
Darf ich mir Ihre Zeitung leihen?
Wir möchten uns gern einige Bücher leihen.

I can't get (myself) used to the climate.
My wife and I can't get (ourselves) used to the climate.
May I borrow (lend myself) your newspaper?
We'd like to borrow (lend ourselves) some books.

The object of a preposition can also refer to the same person as the subject in a sentence:

Er spricht immer nur von sich.
Ich spreche nicht gern von mir.

He always talks only about himself.
I don't like to talk about myself.

Whenever the subject of the sentence is er, sie, Sie or es, or is a noun which can be replaced by these pronouns, the reflexive pronoun form sich occurs as a prepositional object referring to the same person as the subject.  Wherever the subject of the sentence is ich or wir, or is a noun which can be replaced by ich or wir, German uses the regular pronoun forms mich, mir and uns after prepositions in order to refer to the same person as the subject.
